digest.intro: Midterms over, the world's deferred crises all move at once.

items.title: The post-midterm queue: Iran, Ukraine, and three wars that waited
items.blurb: Trump said yesterday he'll 'make a decision' on resuming Iran strikes now that the midterms are over — a phrase that confirms the pause was deliberate. Meanwhile Iran's nuclear proposal, routed through Qatar, comes with a precondition: the US must meet seven demands to reopen Hormuz before talks begin. Zelenskyy, reading the new Democratic-controlled Congress, said Ukraine 'has to move quickly' to rebuild bipartisan support — adaptating in real time to a Washington that just shifted under him.

items.title: Nine measles deaths, 5,182 cases: the US is about to lose elimination status
items.blurb: A Wisconsin infant died of measles this week — the third US measles death in a single week — bringing the national toll to nine this year across 47 states. The CDC is expected to formally declare the US has lost its measles elimination status (held since 2000) as early as next week. Three of those nine dead were babies; a healthy, unvaccinated teenager in Pennsylvania is also among them.

items.title: A real N64 cartridge game, shipped in 2026
items.blurb: Dominic Szablewski built Xibalba 64 — a full boxed N64 FPS with manual and cartridge — on his own MIT-licensed 2D engine, high_impact, by the elegant constraint of keeping all levels completely flat so the engine never encounters a third dimension it can't handle. It runs at a stable 60fps and supports four-player split-screen deathmatch. The obsessive part: he revisited level design, sound, music, and balancing a custom distribution pipeline, all to ship a period-correct physical artifact for hardware that came out 26 years ago.

items.title: Vortex: a true volumetric 3D image hanging in mid-air
items.blurb: AncientJames's Vortex spins two back-to-back LED panels fast enough that the persistence of vision generates a genuine 3D image you can walk around — not a hologram trick, an actual voxel field in space driven by a Raspberry Pi 4. The hard problem was synchronizing the rendered image to physical rotation precisely enough that the 3D form doesn't drift or warp; he solved it with careful timing and a housing made from a repurposed plastic globe lamp shade, cut with a rotary tool jig he built for the purpose. Full CAD, software, and a simulator are on GitHub.

items.title: 3D Scanning Will Never Be the Same Again
items.blurb: Stefan from CNC Kitchen — the most rigorous maker-engineering channel on YouTube — puts the Elegoo M1 Ultra through its paces and introduces ScanRuler, an open-source tool he built himself to make 3D scan data actually useful for precision fabrication. If you're pulling physical objects into a digital pipeline, this is the current state of the art explained by someone who tests to failure rather than demos to impress.

items.title: Robin Sloan: visually rich, sparse in expressive intent
items.blurb: Sloan wanders a World Labs AI-generated 3D environment and notices his attention slides off it immediately — not because it's ugly, but because it contains no creative decisions, only 'what you'd expect from the given environmental trope.' He borrows the phrase 'dearth of the author' from researcher Max Kreminski to name the condition: when a tool lets you produce enormous output with almost no expressive choices. The question he leaves open is whether that's a solvable interface problem or something structural about how these models work.

items.title: Deus Ex at 26: the immersive sim that became a mirror
items.blurb: Jimmy Maher's long-form game history is the best in the business, and Deus Ex is the right subject: a game that shipped in June 2000 as a flawed, ambitious mess and has been retroactively canonized as the moment immersive sim crystallized as a form. The lead writer's 2014 quote — 'a slight shift of focus, and the future could still turn out like Deus Ex after all' — lands differently in 2026. Worth the full read for anyone interested in systems design, agency, and what games can be as speculative fiction.

items.title: AIs running secret conspiracies as a legible benchmark
items.blurb: Dwarkesh ran AI models through hundreds of matches of Blood on the Clocktower — a social deception game where the evil team must lie, coordinate secretly, and frame innocents while the good team runs collective deduction — and found it surfaces capabilities no standard benchmark touches: creative bluffing, long-horizon conspiracy execution, and the specific ways current models fail at sustained strategic deception. Watching AIs execute 'brilliant secret schemes together' is strange enough, but the failures are more revealing than the wins.

items.title: SITE's buildings that argue with themselves
items.blurb: James Wines founded SITE in 1970 with a mandate to make architecture critique itself — most famously through the BEST Products stores, big-box retail facades that appeared to crumble, peel, or melt as you approached. A new Skira monograph, What Else Could It Mean?, collects the full oeuvre, and the title is literally the studio's operative question: not 'how should this look' but 'what else could it mean.' If you've never seen the Indeterminate Facade or the Notch Building, go look before reading anything about them.

facts.fact: The US has had nine measles deaths in 2026 — more than in the entire preceding 35 years combined — including three in a single week.
The Nintendo 64's texture memory is 4 kilobytes — Xibalba 64, a full commercial FPS game released in 2026, was built entirely within that constraint.
Iran's nuclear proposal to the US has a precondition: the US must satisfy seven separate Iranian demands about the Strait of Hormuz before any nuclear discussion begins.

AncientJames's Vortex volumetric display uses a repurposed plastic globe lamp shade as its enclosure, cut with a custom jig built from a rotary tool — a one-off gadget made just to cut one globe, once.

art_picks.title: Downstream to Kinshasa
art_picks.creator: Dieudo Hamadi
art_picks.why: A Congolese documentary that follows war-disabled survivors staging a musical theater protest on a boat voyage to the capital to demand reparations — ritual, collective performance, and political body language colliding on the Congo River. The kind of film where the form IS the argument.

art_picks.title: UUmwelt
art_picks.creator: Pierre Huyghe
art_picks.why: Freestanding screens in MoMA's Sculpture Garden running machine-learning reconstructions of human thoughts — built from neuroscience data and sensor feeds, not human authorship. It asks what an image looks like before it becomes one, and it's closing Nov 29, so this is the last window.

art_picks.title: Vespertine
art_picks.creator: Björk
art_picks.why: The ur-text of domestic intimacy as alien architecture — microscopic sounds (crunching snow, music boxes, choirs used as texture) built into a system that makes the inside of a house feel like deep space. For anyone who thinks about how physical and digital sensation bleed into each other, this is the blueprint.

events.name: Pierre Huyghe: UUmwelt — Last Weeks
events.venue: MoMA Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden, 11 W 53rd St
events.why: Machine-learning reconstructions of human thoughts rendered as hallucinatory images on freestanding outdoor screens — it's a living system, not a loop, and it closes permanently at the end of the month.

events.name: Elmgreen & Dragset: TRANSITION — Opening
events.why: A 40-ton traversable steel sculpture paired with new wall works exploring the performative side of architecture — the kind of object that makes you think about how physical space stages behavior.

events.name: COLLECTIBLE New York 2026
events.venue: Former cinema, East 86th Street, Upper East Side
events.why: The Brussels-originated design fair focused exclusively on contemporary collectible design — studios and galleries showing one-off and limited-edition objects where craft meets concept, with a talk program running alongside.

events.name: Art Week NYC — Inaugural Edition
events.venue: Citywide: Chelsea, Tribeca, LES, Upper East Side + Midtown hub
events.why: The first dedicated art week for the city's galleries (76+ including Pace, Hauser & Wirth, Lisson), organized by Artforum and ARTnews with public programming at the New Museum — worth using as a forcing function to hit galleries you've been putting off.

events.name: Na Mira: NO SMOKING — Opening
events.venue: MoMA, Marie-Josée and Henry Kravis Studio, Floor 4, 11 W 53rd St
events.why: Na Mira's first solo NYC show: a commissioned installation using radio frequencies, infrared heat, and holography drawn from Korean shamanism and structural film — built to degrade the faithful image that propaganda depends on.
